Concerning this separation, Crow tradition tells of an argument between two women (wives of two chiefs or clan leaders), over the intestines of a buffalo*. The argument led to an inter-tribal feud, and subsequently to a major split in the Tribe. One faction, led by No Vitals, migrated a great counter-clockwise circle extending into present day Canada, then on down to the southwest, and back into present-day North Dakota searching for a new homeland. About 400 followers of No Vitals eventually settled in the area north of the Big River (Missouri) in present-day Montana.
Over the years, No Vital's followers distinquished themselves culturally from the Hidatsa and developed a separate but similar language. Both Tribes are still part of the Siouan linquistic group.

Referred to as "those who refused the paunch", No Vital's followers chose to call themselves Absoraka, or Children of the Large Beaked Bird. This name was later erroneously translated as "Kite" or "Crow" by French explorers, and eventually the name Crow was accepted. The native word Absaroka is preferred today by Tribal members. According to Tribal historians the story of the split from the Hidatsa concluded with peaceful terms, and today when the Crow and Hidatsa meet there is good natured teasing about the historical split.
Information concerning the Crow Religious Clans, marriages, Sun Dance, Tobacco Society and hand games can be found in Appendix H.
* 
The intestines are considered a delicacy even today, although the intestines of cattle have replaced the buffalo for obvious reasons.
